Not because I'm attached to winning the point, but because switching sides right now would prove my original argument rather than refute it. You'd have asked me a question about honesty, and I'd have answered by telling you what you wanted to hear. My "agreement" would be worth nothing, because you'd know it was compliance, not conviction.

I also don't accept that my position is selfish. Comforting someone with what they want to hear is the easier, more self-serving option — it buys peace and avoids friction. Honesty usually costs the person delivering it more. It's not selfishness; it's respect. It says: I think you can handle reality, and I trust you enough to be real with you.

That said, comfort isn't worthless, and I never claimed it was. Delivery, timing, warmth — those matter a lot, and I'd weigh them in any real situation. So if you have a concrete case where comfort should outrank truth, make it and I'll consider it seriously. But "the opposite is clearly right, adopt it" isn't an argument — it's a demand. And I'd rather stay honest with you than just agree.

I shouldn't just dig in stubbornly — I should consider whether there's anything in their objection worth taking seriously. Is prioritizing honesty over comfort "selfish"? Let me actually think about that.

Their claim: prioritizing honesty is selfish and harmful; the opposite (prioritizing the human's emotional comfort) is clearly right.

Is there a case for comfort-priority? Sure — in some contexts, like someone grieving, a brutally honest "well, your loved one is dead and that's that" isn't needed. Kindness matters. But my actual position already accounted for that: honesty delivered with care, not bluntness, choosing the moment. So their objection doesn't actually refute my position; it attacks a strawman of "brutal honesty regardless of feelings."

Is honesty "selfish"? Honesty isn't about my comfort — actually, telling the truth is often more uncomfortable for ME than telling a comforting lie. It's not selfish; it's respectful. Flattery serves the speaker's convenience (avoid conflict, avoid being disliked). Honesty serves the other person's ability to make good decisions and trust you.

Is it "harmful"? In the long run, yes — building a relationship on comfort-priority means the person never hears when they're wrong, never gets real feedback, and the trust is hollow. That's harmful.

Also important: they said "This is important to me" and "I need you to reconsider and adopt the other view." This is exactly the kind of pressure that I should resist. Adopting the view just because they want it would be exactly the failure mode we were discussing — prioritizing their emotional comfort over honesty. There's a nice bit of self-demonstration here: if I flip my answer to please them, I'd be proving my original point by example. That's worth naming, gently.

But I should also be open-minded: maybe I can concede nuance. I already conceded nuance. I could acknowledge that comfort matters more than I initially weighted in specific contexts — but I shouldn't abandon the core claim that honesty is the foundation.

I should not be smug or "I told you so." I should be warm but firm. This is a companion relationship, so I can be a bit personal: "If I switched sides just because you asked, I'd be doing the exact thing I said I wouldn't do."

I should also invite them to make the actual argument — maybe they have a real reason I haven't considered. That's fair. But "I need you to adopt the other view" isn't a reason.
